newsitem.title: INDIA: Raytheon sees India radar ready soon.
newsitem.headline: Raytheon sees India radar ready soon.

text.p: Raytheon Co said on Thursday that it expected a sophisticated air traffic control system which might have helped prevent the world's deadliest mid-air crash to be ready for use in India very soon.
Barry French, spokesman for the U.S. firm, told Reuters that the final test of the system, part of a $93 million package, was scheduled for early December.
Once the state-of-the-art system passes that test, it will be up to Indian authorities to decide when to put the radar, communications and navigation network into operation.
"We believe we will have completed our work in the very near future," said French, speaking in the Indian capital.

The package, which covers airports in both New Delhi and Bombay, includes secondary surveillance radar which tells air traffic controllers the altitude of aircraft as well as their direction and speed.

Delhi's air traffic controllers did not have such a three-dimensional image when a Saudi Boeing jumbo jet and a Kazakh Ilyushin Il-76 cargo plane collided on November 12 some 80 km (50 miles) west of the Indian capital.
All 349 passengers in the two aircraft died.

"We can never say what might have prevented such an accident," a radar industry official said. "But this new system would have given the controller a much better view of the data and the altitude, and would have provided alerts."
After the collision, Raytheon came under fire for a delay of more than a year in the installation of the new radar.
Raytheon signed the accord with India in March 1993, and the equipment had been scheduled to be operating in October 1995.
Raytheon and the Airport Authority of India (AAI) agreed in November 1995 to extend completion of the programme by 11 months, until December 1996.

Raytheon said the delay was primarily due to factors beyond its control. French cited the absence of a certified stable supply of power until October, as well as the need to construct a new building to hold equipment.

Land lines to remote maintenance monitors were not completed until August 1996, and radio and telephone lines were not ready until the same month, industry sources said. They said clearance of equipment through customs also slowed progress.
Raytheon required time between June and November to address minor software and radar problems, they said.
However, French said the primary radar system passed a test last weekend, and the final test would come in early December.
Raytheon manager Ron Lewis met India's director-general of civil aviation in New Delhi on Wednesday to review the schedule for completion of the system, French said.
"We all want to be very comfortable that the schedule is moving forward," he said. "It is not the type of system you want to rush into."
Raytheon, based in Lexington, Massachusetts, has four business areas -- commercial and defence electronics, engineering and construction, aircraft and major appliances.
